title: Creamy Truffle Tagliatelle with Porcini
summary: Tagliatelle in a silky sauce of dried porcini, white wine, truffle paste and Parmesan, with a little chilli. Rich, but not heavy with cream.

steps.heading: Soak the porcini
steps.text: Put the porcini in a bowl and pour over the warm water, enough to cover them. Leave for {timer:20-25|porcini}, until soft.

Lift the porcini out and squeeze out the excess liquid gently. Do not throw away the soaking water: strain it through a coffee filter, or a fine sieve lined with kitchen paper, to remove any grit. Measure out the strained soaking liquid the sauce needs.
Cut the larger porcini into bite-sized pieces, leaving some whole for texture.

steps.heading: Prepare
steps.text: While the porcini soak, finely mince the garlic, finely chop the parsley (keeping a little for the top) and finely grate the Parmesan.
Measure out the wine, the Elmlea and the truffle paste, and divide the butter in half. Put a large pot of water on to heat.

steps.heading: Fry the porcini
steps.text: Heat a large, deep frying pan over a medium-high heat. Add the olive oil and half the butter.
Once the butter has melted, add the drained porcini and fry for {timer:5-6}, stirring occasionally, until the moisture has gone and they take on a little colour.
Turn the heat down to medium-low. Add the garlic and the chilli flakes and cook for {timer:45-60s}, stirring constantly so the garlic does not burn.

steps.heading: Deglaze
steps.text: Turn the heat up to medium and pour in the wine, scraping the bottom of the pan to lift any browned bits. Simmer for {timer:3-4}, until reduced by about two-thirds.
Add the strained soaking liquid and simmer for another {timer:2}. The base should smell deeply of mushrooms, with a little acidity from the wine.

steps.heading: Cream and butter
steps.text: Turn the heat down to medium-low. Pour in the Elmlea, add the rest of the butter and stir until it melts and the sauce is smooth. Season with black pepper and simmer gently for {timer:2}. It may look a little loose: the pasta starch and the Parmesan will thicken it.

steps.heading: The truffle
steps.text: Turn off the heat and stir in the truffle paste, keeping back about a teaspoon, until evenly mixed. Taste, and add the rest for a stronger truffle flavour. Do not boil the sauce once the truffle paste is in.

steps.heading: Cook the tagliatelle
steps.text: Ideally, start the pasta while the sauce is cooking so they finish together. Bring a very large pot of water to a rolling boil and salt it well, a little less if your truffle paste and Parmesan are salty.
Add the tagliatelle and stir straight away so it does not stick. Cook until about 1 minute before al dente, by the packet.
Keep a large mugful of the pasta water, then drain the pasta without rinsing it.

steps.heading: Bring it together
steps.text: Add the tagliatelle straight to the sauce with a good splash of the pasta water, and toss gently over a very low heat for {timer:30-60s}.
Turn off the heat. Add the Parmesan gradually, tossing all the time. If the sauce is too thick, add more pasta water, a splash at a time, and keep tossing until it is silky and coats every strand.
Stir in most of the parsley, then taste and adjust the salt, pepper and chilli. Leave it a little saucier than you think it needs: it soaks up sauce as you serve.

steps.heading: Serve
steps.text: Divide between warm plates, making sure everyone gets plenty of porcini, and finish with the rest of the parsley, a little extra Parmesan and black pepper.

tips: Keep the truffle aroma: add the paste off the heat, after the wine has reduced and the cream is in.
Do not let the sauce get too thick. There is little cream for this much pasta, so the pasta water matters: add it gradually to keep the sauce silky.
Have the Parmesan grated, the parsley chopped and the plates ready before you drain the pasta, so nothing sits around getting cold.
As a guide, boil about 1 litre of water for every 100 g of pasta, salted with about 6 g of salt.
